tip: X of Y takes two suffixes: ‘-in’ on the owner, ‘-i’ on the thing. ‘dersin konusu’ means the lesson's subject.
‘yüzünden’ means because of and is usually used for unwanted causes. ‘yağmur yüzünden’ means because of the rain.
‘henüz’ plus a negative past verb means not yet. ‘henüz pasaportumu almadım’ means I haven't gotten my passport yet.
‘kadar’ after a place in the -a form (the to-ending) means as far as. ‘ormana kadar’ means all the way to the forest.
The ‘-ir’ ending marks habits and general truths. ‘pişirir’ means bakes, as in bakes fresh bread every morning.
Ranking numbers (third, fourth) add ‘-üncü/-ıncı’. ‘üç’ is three, ‘üçüncü’ is third, as in ‘üçüncü katında’, on the third floor.
‘çünkü’ (because) is unusual for Turkish: it sits before its reason clause. ‘çünkü zamanım vardı’ means because I had time.
The suffix ‘-malı/-meli’ means must or should. ‘al’ (get) plus ‘-malıyım’ gives ‘almalıyım’, I must get.
The ending ‘-dir’ gives a statement a general, factual tone. ‘meyvedir’ means is a fruit, stated as a plain fact.
The from-ending ‘-dan/-den’ means from. ‘fırın’ (bakery) plus ‘-dan’ gives ‘fırından’, from the bakery.
‘bulamadım’ = ‘bul’ (find) + ‘ama’ (cannot) + ‘dım’ (I did): I couldn't find. The ‘-ama-’ part marks inability, separate from the plain negative.
‘geçen’ means the one that passed, so ‘geçen ay’ is last month and ‘geçen hafta’ is last week. It sits before the time word.
‘hazırlanmak’ (to prepare) attaches what you prepare for with ‘-a’ (the to-form), so you get ready ‘sınava’, for the exam, not ‘sınavı’.
‘yapmayı’ is ‘yap’ (do) + ‘ma’ (the act of) + ‘yı’ (object mark): the cooking becomes the thing learned. Verbs turn into objects this way.
‘almadan’ = ‘al’ (take) + ‘madan’: without taking. Add ‘-madan’ to a verb stem to say without doing that action.
‘gürültüden’ uses the from-ending ‘-den’ to give the cause: because of the noise. ‘-den’ can mean from or, as here, due to.
‘öğrenci’ is ‘öğren’ (learn) + ‘ci’: one who does it, a learner. The ‘-ci’ ending names the person tied to the action or thing.
‘Ramazan'da’ takes an apostrophe before the suffix because ‘Ramazan’ is a proper name: ‘Ramazan’ + ‘da’ becomes ‘Ramazan'da’.
Clock times take the ‘-de’ ending for at: ‘yedide’ means at seven. So ‘saat yedide’ is at seven o'clock.
‘şehir’ drops its second vowel before an ending that starts with a vowel, so ‘şehir’ + ‘imiz’ + ‘de’ becomes ‘şehrimizde’, in our city, not ‘şehirimizde’.
‘çıkmadan önce’ means before going. Use verb stem + ‘madan önce’ for before doing something: ‘çıkmadan önce’, before leaving.
‘sucuklu’ is ‘sucuk’ + ‘lu’: with sucuk. The ‘-lu’ ending, also ‘-lı, -li, -lü’, means having or served with that thing.
‘soran’ is ‘sor’ (ask) + ‘an’: the one who asks. Add ‘-an/-en’ to a verb to name the doer, like ‘eden’, the one who does.
‘almam gerekiyor’ means I need to take. Build it as verb + ‘ma’ + my + ‘gerekiyor’, so the need is personal: my taking is needed.
‘görmek’ here means to receive, not to see. ‘saygı görür’ is gets respect, the same pattern as ‘ilgi görmek’, to get attention.
‘yapıyorlar’ with no named subject means they in the general sense, like people make. It often reads as food is made here.
‘market’ ends in a hard t, so the from-ending hardens to ‘-ten’, not ‘-den’: ‘marketten’, from the market.
‘izlerdi’ is ‘izle’ + ‘r’ + ‘di’: used to watch. The ‘-rdi’ ending marks a repeated past habit, not a single event.
‘korkmak’ pairs with the from-ending ‘-den’ for what scares you: ‘şeyden korkmaz’ means fears nothing, literally not afraid from anything.
‘kaynar’ is ‘kayna’ + ‘r’, the ‘-r’ ending for a general truth: water boils, always. This ending states facts and habits, not one moment.
